The authors leverage a transformer architecture, which is well-suited for capturing long-range dependencies in sequential data, and adapt it to the specific challenges of ODE inference. A key aspect of their approach is the use of a numerical integration scheme to generate training data, which allows them to create a large dataset of ODEs with known solutions. This dataset, ODEBench, is presented as a valuable resource for the community. The model is trained to predict the symbolic representation of the ODE, such as a polynomial or trigonometric expression, given a time series of observations. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of ODEFormer through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showing that it outperforms existing methods in terms of robustness to noise and irregular sampling, while also maintaining computational efficiency. The paper also includes a discussion of the limitations of the current approach, such as the restriction to first-order ODEs, and suggests directions for future research. Overall, this work presents a significant step towards automating the discovery of physical laws from data, which has the potential to accelerate scientific discovery in various fields. The paper is well-written and easy to follow, making it accessible to a broad audience. The authors have also made their code and benchmark dataset publicly available, which will facilitate further research in this area.
